Title: Massachusetts Institute of Eggs
Author: Leanne F. '30
Article Content: One uneventful morning, I sat eating a breakfast of quiche with a side of hard boiled eggs accompanied by a pile of scrambled egg, chased down with an egg-coated bread (french toast). My friend across from me chomped on an omelet. It occured to me that we eat tons of eggs at MIT. I eat probably 3-4 a day, and since ~42 days have passed, I’ve eaten ~150 eggs so far. I will have eaten ~750 eggs by the end of my first year. With this eggstensive experience, it would be a waste to not rank them! General MIT egg⁠01Fun fact: eggs are a near perfect food! They have a full amino acid profile, almost every essential vitamin the body needs, choline, healthy fats, and antioxidants.stats: All eggs are cage free, if that matters to you. My mom’s super meticulous about eggs, but to me eggs are eggs. I’m not falling for the free-range pasture-raised antibiotic -free propaganda. MIT carries white, brown, and bagged liquid eggs. I’m judging on : Taste Presentation Availability in dining halls (because if we can’t get them then what’s even the point …but the the final # of egg stars/ ranking is based on my holistic vibey determination of what I like, unrelated to subcategory scores S- tier: Shakshuka egg- STOP THE PICTURE MAKES IT LOOK SO BAD I SWEAR IT WAS GOOD there in the far corner! this is not helping my case. Here's a pic form Bon Appetit of what it should look like An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next I am completely biased. I am such a sucker for shakshuka. Yes, I know the photo looks chopped. But the mixture of tomato + feta + runny egg is so good. I would do unspeakable things for a good shakshuka. Unfortunately, this one is mid, but in my mind even a mid shakshuka is an S. Taste: 5/5 The eggs were runny and it was actually seasoned well! It totally felt and tasted like canned tomatoes, though. Basil and feta was a nice touch Presentation: 1/5 Bro. Just look at it. It looks like shakshuka after I digested it for an hour. I would eat tasty slop anyday though! Availability: 1/5 Genuinely a shiny pokemon. I saw her twice and never again. Can we petition for more shakshuka :( And it ran out so fast… Fried egg- A classic! You kinda gotta get lucky with how well the chefs cook your egg, though. You can also ask for any cook type (sunny side up, over easy/medium/hard) . My go-to is a sunny side up for the runny dippable yolk. and if you order over-hard eggs… I’m silently judging you. Taste: 4.5/5 Not much to say, fried eggs are always good! Crispy edges and super hot and fresh. Sunny side ups are always a little raw, but the salmonella risk is so worth it to me. Presentation: 5/5 LOOK HOW PRETTY Availability: 4/5 You can get them at any omelet station, and they’re speedier than omelets A- Tier: Omelet- An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Most dining halls at MIT have an omelet station for breakfast and brunch. They have tons of toppings like ham and veggies and cheese, and in Vassar they let you cook your own! There’s also supposedly a famous omelet chef in Vassar who makes elite omelets, but I’ve yet to try one. Taste: 4.5/5 It’s so nice having a hearty fat hot veggie egg dish in the morning Unseasoned so season on your own Sometimes too oily ITS HUGE Presentation: 3/5 But I don’t think anyone is ordering an omelet for the looks. IMO, pretty omelets don’t (and shouldn’t) exist! Availability: 3/5 Sometimes there’s a bit of a wait, but generally I can get an omelet in <5 minutes Fluffy scrambled egg (with cheese): The best scramble you can find at MIT! You can get it cheesed or un-cheesed, and these are the least dry, most standard scrambled egg (they get so much worse). Shoutout to my friend Will for letting me taste test his eggs because I was too lazy to wait in line for them. Taste: 4/5 A nice, standard scramble, made of bagged eggs. salt it urself Presentation: 4/5 Like omelets, scrambled eggs are always a lil chopped. Still, this is the prettiest scramble you’re gonna get here… under the heaters they look like piles of gold Availability: 5/5 Always at vassar brunch! B- Tier: average Quiche (broccoli and cheddar): Another quiche variation An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Quiche is just mid in general? Like I’ve never had a life changing quiche. This isn’t the best quiche I’ve had but it’s not bad! Taste: 3.5/5 It tastes and looks like an egg pie with broccoli and cheese. Needs salt The cheese forms a hard dry layer Crust is good though Presentation: 3.5/5 Its holey Availability: 3/5 I see it 1-2x a week at Simmons Dining, sometimes at Vassar. Sometimes triangle and sometimes square form Microwaved sunny side up: the MIT way- finished product yolk reveal wax paper for easy cleanup! An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next News about people getting their faces blasted by exploding microwaved egg particles has given me an irrational fear of microwaving eggs…. But! my fellow blogger Sara put me on to this method, which hasn’t exploded on her yet! “I crack open two eggs on a stack of three paper plates and toss it in the microwave for idk how long but I go in 30 sec increments. Boom fried egg.” I microwaved my egg for 1 min total as I stood in the opposite corner of the room, just to be safe. There was a lot of ominous popping going on in the microwave, but it turned out okay. (I still need to try other blogger egg recipes, like Vera’s domino pizza omelet and Petey’s microwave scramble.) Taste: 4/5 NGL it was surprisingly similar to a fried egg , just without the fry, and I kinda achieved a runny yolk The sides of the egg overcooked and got rubbery though. Next time I would use a little bowl instead of a plate or add some water to prevent this Next time I’d also center the yolk so it doesn’t overcook while waiting for the whites to cook. Presentation: 4/5 Some minor explosions but not bad! Availability: 5/5 It just took a minute plus no cleanup. Way easier than boiling or frying my own eggs. Would use this method again if short on time. Hot hard boiled egg- An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next There’s a strange sense of joy and fulfillment that comes with eating a nice hot hard boiled egg with salt and pepper. Plus, they’re very portable, and ours are relatively easy to peel! Taste: 4/5 I’ve never had to deal with the weird sulfury smell some boiled eggs get. It’s SUPER well cooked though, and imo, soft boil >>hard boil Presentation: 3/5 Grey yolk is kinda nasty The beautiful pristine piles of eggs give me joy Availability: 4/5 Always there at brunch, sometimes during the week. Egg salad- An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next ewww egg saladdd I hate mayo. But I sometimes see people with full bowls piled with this stuff, so there’s some demand i guess Taste: 4/5 Standard egg + mayo flavor, with nice evenly sized chunks of egg white dispersed throughout sometimes if you’re lucky they’ll add parsley! wow! Presentation: 3.5/5 I’m realizing that egg dishes are maybe just always chopped. I’ve definitely seen ugly egg salads, though, and ours actually look to be on the appealing side of the spectrum Availability: 3/5 Unremarkable so I never pay attention to it Cold hard boiled egg: An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Pre-peeled, so you can get quick protein for mega gains! I see a lot of people eating these, but imo they’re just boring, and there’s always some better form of egg to eat. Taste: 4/5 Exactly how you’d expect. Needs sauce Presentation: 3/5 Sometimes they’re suspiciously deformed and dented. Can’t blame them. sometimes I feel like a deformed cold boiled egg too. Availability: 5/5 Almost always at the salad bar! C-Tier: would not eat unless no other option… Layered scrambled egg An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next This is the scramble method where they make flat crepe-like layers and just stack them to make a scramble. The extra surface area makes it super dry and rubbery. Taste: 2.5/5 Dryyyy, weirddd. flavorlessss. When I get desperate and have to eat it, I DOUSE it in ketchup It’s also somehow wet and soggy at the same time. Pools of liquid collect at the bottom Presentation: 2/5 Yellow layered brick that you carve/shave chunks out of Availability: 3/5 Lets bring that number down D-Tier: how do you even achieve this form of egg Powdered scrambled egg An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Like egg gravel. Egg pellets. Idk if we can even consider this a scrambled egg Taste: 2.5/5 Imagine eating dry rice-like egg chunks. You sort of have to dig past a crusty dry layer to get to the edible parts, which you then discover are also hard and dry. The ketchup to-egg-ratio I need to use is kind of horrifying. Presentation: 1/5 I’m getting the ick. Availability: 2/5 Not often seen in simmons but it’s a sad day when I do The eggs I’d dream of seeing at MIT: soft boiled, poached. Omg. eggs benedict. I can only dream… That’s the end of my ranking so far! The dining staff has been giving me a lot of concerned looks because I keep taking pictures of their eggs. I need a break! I might do a follow up later in the year with more eggs and more egg expertise. I’d love to hear of any disagreements anyone might have as well. I usually have pretty controversial food takes.

Title: How to cure a cough
Author: Allison E. '27
Article Content: The freshman flu has long since arrived, and it will be longer yet til it releases its talons from student bodies across the country. A couple of weeks ago, like many of my compatriots, I too fell victim to the plague. I had mostly mild symptoms that disappeared quickly, but for some reason, the terrible, hacking cough that was scaring my suitemates never got the memo. It continued for weeks, long after I’d recovered from the cold. In that time, I learned many things about coughing: A single awkwardly positioned cough can lead to a badly pulled muscle, which then makes all subsequent coughing (and also walking or sitting up or existing) rather painful. Talking, and especially singing, is very difficult, and it can make your cough worse for hours even after you’ve shut up. Usually coughing satiates the urge to cough, but there’s a particularly annoying type of throat tickle where coughing just makes it worse, and then you feel like a cotton ball monster is climbing down your throat trying to choke you. Do not recommend. If you’re coughing hard enough, you can compress your stomach so much that you throw up. This was a daily occurrence for a while. In attempting to deal with these, I tried many, many different ways to suppress the cough enough to go about everyday life. Some of them prescribed by urgent care, and some of them prescribed by… my imagination. Anyways, in an effort to make some small amount of lemonade⁠01omg wait I should’ve tried this as a cough remedy too from my ailments, I now present to you the results of my incredibly unscientific study of the cough-remedy-space. 1. Masks Even though I wasn’t contagious after the first week or so (according to urgent care), most people around me didn’t know that, and I was hacking non-stop everywhere I went. I was truly a public menace, so I wore the mask for other people’s peace of mind. But! The mask also helped keep the air I was breathing moist, which kept any dry-throat coughs at bay. 7/10 2. Cough drops I went through at least four family sized bags of cough drops⁠02There are few pharmacy items that I buy from name brand, but when I’m coughing, I’m willing to shell out for the Ricola lemon mint cough drops. They taste great, and more importantly, they have less menthol in them, so I can use more of them without getting a stomach ache. in a month. These are particularly useful when trying to sing–they don’t make the cough go away, but they do help. For several choir rehearsals, I was basically just chain smoking cough drops the whole way through–as soon as one was finished, or sometimes even before, I’d pop another one. This rounds out to about 12 cough drops per 2.5 hr rehearsal. Mildly concerning? Yes. Did my stomach hurt after? Also yes. But it did prevent me from coughing every 30 seconds. 9/10 3. Hi-Chew I ran out of cough drops at the same time our on-campus grocery store also ran out, so I replaced them with Hi-Chew. These do not work as well as cough drops, and don’t last as long, but they’re sufficient in cases of emergency. Also they taste good. 5/10 4. Gum To avoid consuming 30 Hi-Chew (and 90g of sugar) per day, I introduced a second cough drop replacement: chewing gum. This one actually works shockingly well, partly because the gum is minty, but I think mainly because it encourages saliva production for as long as you’re chewing it. Only downside is that my jaw gets tight if I chew too much. I did once try both gum and Hi-Chew at the same time during choir rehearsal. As you might expect, the flavors and textures blend quite poorly, and a nontrivial amount of gum probably got swallowed with the Hi-Chew. I do not recommend this combination. 8/10 5. Sleep I was very careful about averaging ~8 hours of sleep per night, and I assume this broadly helped. Difficult to isolate the effect, though. ?/10 6. Honey lemon ginger tea Over the course of these weeks, my wonderful roommate⁠03or, used to be roommate, but we still live in the same suite and also she deserves a grander title than ‘friend’ Miranda made me an egregious quantity of honey lemon ginger tea. This one is probably the holy grail of all cough remedies–the honey coats your throat to prevent the tickle, and I have absolutely no clue what the lemon and ginger do but somehow they are also soothing. The only reason I didn’t use this 24/7 is that the tea is tricky to transport and keep warm, and also I can only steal so much of Miranda’s groceries before I turn into a goblin. 10/10 7. Black milk tea with honey My alternative to honey lemon ginger tea that does not deplete Miranda’s supply of groceries. Still has honey, but I could definitely tell the difference without lemon or ginger. 7/10 8. Straight honey, poured onto a spoon Sometimes I was too lazy to make tea, and sometimes I needed a super-concentrated hit to get me through a particularly bad bout of coughing. I managed to go through half a bottle of honey in a week and a half. Miranda was slightly appalled. But it works! Also I once brought the entire bottle to a rehearsal and poured it straight into my mouth. 9.5/10 9. Dextromethrophan, aka Delsym I was taking this for a long time, and I think?? it helped a little bit, but not much. Lowkey though I like the way the grape liquid tastes. 5/10 10. Guaifenesin, aka Mucinex I tried this one too, but didn’t really notice any effects. Also it tastes worse. 3/10 11. Being silent A rather difficult proposition in everyday life, especially when you have classes and choir rehearsals. But when I did employ it, it actually made a big difference. It just also made me sad, because I like yapping. 6/10 12. Soup This was not as effective as it has been for me in the past. Nevertheless, good soup. 5/10 13. Pseudoephedrine hydrochloride I got this one prescribed on my first urgent care visit, tried it just a couple times, and it didn’t do anything for me. Probably works very well in other cases, just didn’t happen to in mine. This feels too medical for me to have an opinion / 10 14. Benzonatate Basically the same thing as 11. I am not a doctor I do not make medical recommendations / 10 15. Neti-pot If you’ve never heard of a neti-pot, it’s literally just pouring water through your nose to flush your sinuses. It is truly a fascinating experience to pour warm, salty water through one nostril and watch it come out the other. Lowkey less unpleasant than I thought it’d be. A lot of people absolutely swear by this, and it definitely helped me some, but not as much as I hoped. 7/10 16. Water Oops this should probably be #1 but I lowkey forgot about it. Great for temporary relief (i.e. while you’re actively swallowing but not necessarily after), but generally not too effective for me. Very good for bodily and immune function though! 8/10 17. Albuterol inhaler I think this is one of the canonical asthma inhalers? Also prescribed by urgent care. We were definitely going for the shotgun approach with these prescriptions, because nobody knew what was going on (I guess this is not uncommon for coughs). Took me a bit to figure out how to use it, and I didn’t really notice an effect. Please consult your physician / 10 18. Ipratripium bromide inhaler By the time I was prescribed this inhaler, I was getting kinda desperate. I think it helped a little bit, but by this point it might’ve been placebo. Also for some reason this one tasted like green apple??? I didn’t even know there were multiple kinds of inhalers / 10 19. Smoothie Lowkey the same as water, but tasty. I guess the cold also helps a bit. I just wanted more excuse to make smoothie. Plus you can add honey. 8/10 Intermission. Things I considered but did not try: Antibiotics bought over-the-counter outside the US, offered by one of my friends, which I almost took until my mom yelled at me Hungarian cough medicines that I had to google, but unfortunately there were some possible interactions with my other medications Handstands⁠04I can't even do a handstand Giving up on all classes and becoming a hermit I think I probably would have tried all of these, BUT! Finally, finally, finally, I found something that worked. 20. Fluticasone nasal spray, aka Flonase Apparently. The solution this whole time. Was Flonase. Which I could’ve bought WEEKS AGO and without needing urgent care because it’s OVER THE COUNTER. I’ve literally taken Flonase for allergies before. I could’ve been taking it this entire time. AUGH. Flonase takes a while to build up/kick in, but now that I’ve been taking it a while, my cough is almost entirely gone. I am very very grateful. But also a little miffed. What do you mean I was throwing up every night and the solution this whole time was FLONASE. Mildly infuriating. Anyways. I guess this is just a PSA in favor of the shotgun approach to cough remedies. The wonders of modern medicine! Also, big shoutout to the last remedy, which I only had the chance to do after the cough subsided: 21. GET VACCINATED plsplsplsplspls get your flu shot and your COVID shot if you can :D

Title: an arrangement i worked on for video game orchestra!
Author: Victor D. '27
Article Content: I used to play a lot of Pokemon on my DS back when I was a kid. When I got to MIT and found out there’s a whole (Video Game) Orchestra for not only playing but also arranging video game music I was rapt: I had to join, especially since I needed an outlet to continue playing music (I was in band and orchestra in high school). This past summer, I worked on a chamber group arrangement I wrote for Video Game Orchestra! Video Game Orchestra is a completely student-run ensemble of around 60 members. All music we play in VGO is arranged by members of the ensemble! We’re a bit of an eclectic group (in many ways) but especially in our instrumentation: we have a drum set (not typical of traditional orchestras but common enough in video game music), saxophones, euphonium, and guitarists. I really enjoy this though, and for my full group arrangements, I try to leverage all these instruments for unique orchestral textures. For now though, I’ll focus on one of the small groups we’ll be performing at our fall semester concert in December, an octet featuring oboe, celesta, piano, two violins, viola, cello, and bass. Specifically, it’s an arrangement of Floaroma town from Pokemon Diamond Pearl Platinum, one of my favorite game soundtracks of all time. Considering I’ve been drowning in a wave of nostalgia lately, with my recent move back to MIT after spending a summer in home state of California (and also coming to terms that this will be my last year as an undergrad…), this song is very fitting. How does one go about arranging something like this? Well, for me I first listen to the song obsessively then transcribe it. Even before I have a more-or-less faithful transcription though, I already have a decent idea of how I want to reshape the piece, usually starting with instrumentation extensions or substitutions (I substituted the main melody instrument for an oboe from what I interpret as a clarinet in the original, celesta, cello/bass, or piano variously for harp, and oboe for pizzicato violin for instance). I also have my stylistic influences… Been in a rather romantic, sentimental mood. And way too obsessed with Czech Romantic music (Janacek and Dvorak beloveds). So for this arrangement, I was inspired by Dvorak, particularly the 8 Humoresques and Ohlas pisni (Echo of Songs)—the latter determined my choice to feature viola prominently and have it introduce the main melody. Dvorak’s Nocturne was also the primary inspiration for the muted string texture at the beginning and end of the piece: slow, somber sailing punctuated by the double bass’ pizzicato an octave below the bowed cello. Finally, I was thinking of Janacek’s Idyll when developing the ostinatto patterns when the main theme reoccurs the second time. You can listen to a mock-up of the arrangement here [I’ll replace this with a link to the performance which will be in December :3]: Audio Player 00:00 00:00 00:00 Use Up/Down Arrow keys to increase or decrease volume. It should be ready to play! question mark? Though considering the key though… it may benefit from being transposed a half step up or down. We will see at our first rehearsal (which i will go schedule expeditiously rn )

Title: A Witch Stabbed Me
Author: Aiden H. '28
Article Content: This past week, we were graced with an amazing/beautiful/astounding/radiant/etc. three-day weekend. Naturally, given an extra day without nothing I have to do, there was no better answer than doing something that I wouldn’t normally have time for! In this instance, that meant visiting Salem, MA in the peak of October.⁠01Peak here meaning both for Salem and MIT midterms After my friend Fatimeh A.G. ’27 floated the idea in our floor group chat, I jumped at the opportunity to spend a day frolicking around Halloween-ville. Here’s some pictures and stories from that day: 9:00 AM The group of us going met in the floor lounge at the very-early hour of 9-AM-on-a-weekend-*gasp*. Salem is accessible by a ~30 minute ride on the commuter rail, so to be able to get there early enough to spend most of the day there, we had to leave at 9 and perform the following maneuver: Walk to the MIT T ⁠02Short for the MBTA, or Boston's public transit/subway system. stop. Take two stops on the Ashmont/Braintree line until Park Street Transfer to the Green Line Take three stops on the Union St. line until North Station Transfer to the commuter rail station inside North Station This is honestly not that bad of a T experience, but in order to get on the 10:00 train to Salem and teach the freshman how to navigate the T, we had to take our time. While waiting for the train, we were bombarded with Halloween capitalist Dunkin’ before finally getting aboard: An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next After some light gossiping, day planning, and psetting on the ride, we finally emerged from the commuter rail into Salem! We didn’t have any plans for the day, so we started by following the mass of tourists out of the station to what is apparently the town square/downtown, where most of the festivities were: An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Pushing through the crowds of people and noticing that the lines for anything Halloween-related would be at least and hour, we quickly settled on exploring the bookstore to our right instead. I was finally able to find Theo of Golden, which is having a big moment and my grandma volun-told me to buy. Kat E. '30 and Ava A. '30 in the bookstore! An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Starting at this point I was lethally hungry, so I passive-aggressively redirected everyone through the town out of the city center to a random cafe for me to fuel up or whatever. On this walk, we were able to pass through the Salem Common, which had Halloween vendors and decorations set up! An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next matcha and two egg and cheese, tyvm this cafe was crazy An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next We took a look at Google Maps and noticed that we were caddy-corner to the House of Seven Gables, aka the subject of Nathaniel Hawthorne’s book (he is from Salem). We took the detour, and naturally because nature knows when I need amazing vibes and a good photo, the weather became the perfect 70 degrees and sunny at this time: An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Down the street from the house is a path into the middle-ish of the water and a lighthouse, so we decided to take a group break, sit around the water, and gossip and breathe in the ocean air. (this was the best part I love the ocean I am moana/aquaman/waterboy) Emma H. and Meg H. '29 walking to the water with me! An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next We had no other plans for the rest of day, so we commenced a random walk⁠036.100B is ruining me around the city before stumbling upon a bakery/cafe and you KNOW my ass got an apple cider donut (it was perfect): An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Now for the fun part: noticing we had time and having floated around the idea of getting our ears pierced as a floor, Fatimeh, Meg and I went to a local piercer. ‘Twas a super cute store, despite being ridiculously expensive, and we got the coolest helix piercings: Meg's helix! It's a lightning bolt An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next To end the day, we just walked around random shops, and I was able to find a thank you card for a professor and a cute bird postcard for my girlfriend: An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Honestly, I don’t have any intense/philosophical thoughts on the day. Above all, it was just really good vibes to be able to leave campus for a little bit, be with a bunch of friends, and walk around somewhere new where we have nothing to do. Def recommend!

Title: Professor Justin Solomon on AI, math, and education
Author: Chris Peterson SM '13
Article Content: I’m a longtime dedicated listener to the Odd Lots podcast from Bloomberg, which covers finance, markets, technology, economics, and weird little supply chain facts. So imagine my delight when I opened my feed last week and saw MIT’s own Professor Justin Solomon – Associate Dean of Engineering Education and member of the Committee on Undergraduate Admissions & Financial Aid that advises our work — as a guest! I thought it was worth sharing here because I always appreciate hearing Justin’s thoughts on education, science, and intellectual integrity (and not just because he’s a fellow bald bearded guy who wears sport coats sans ties and goes to the Z). The first 50 minutes or so are about math, research, and AI generally; minutes 50-58 or so are about those things and the MIT education specifically (the audio version has more). Hope some of our readers enjoy it too.

Title: free listening
Author: Caleb M. '27
Article Content: It’s a sunny day in Cambridge. It hasn’t rained in a few days, so the stone of campus is dry, and the MIT population mills about to its various hotspots by way of everyone’s favorite junction: Lobby 7. It’s around 5 PM, and the sun is getting lower in the sky. The sky is clear, the world is warm, and you stand on the West side of Mass Ave facing the Little Dome, ready to walk onto campus for… whatever you might need to do that day. It’s a moment like this in which, if you’re lucky, you’ll find yourself glancing down to the corner of the steps by one of the carved MASSACHVSETTS / 77 / AVENVEs and seeing a very particular man sitting there. If alone, he’s likely to be reading a book silently, locked in his own scene as the world drifts around him. If he’s with someone, you’ll find him either intently focused on what they’re sharing with him or gently, carefully responding to what they brought to him. And what they might bring varies vastly: it could be light-hearted or heavy, past problems or future worries, jokes, questions, or just chats. But they’re all tied together by his listening ear and perceptive mind, just as every time you encounter him will be tied together with one very particular object: a white poster-board sign leaning on his knee that reads, in big blue letters: FREE LISTENING. To many, he’s a myth, a character appearing randomly on campus with his unassuming demeanor and quiet stillness invoking a certain mysterious aura about him. To others, he’s just some Bostonian who sits around MIT campus with his weird sign and does… something? To most, however (around campus, at least), he’s known as The Free Listening Guy. “He’s the guy with the Free Listening sign.” Creative title, I know. Everybody probably knows somebody who’s talked to him before, and he comes up in passing conversations as another landmark of MIT’s eclectic environment. Most people are able to deduce that he’s there for you to come and talk to, and that (as his sign reads) he’ll listen. Seems like an interesting outlet, I guess, especially at a place like MIT where there seems to always be something to get off your chest. Lots of people think he won’t talk back, just sit there like a wall for you to bounce your thoughts off of, but does anyone really know? But I’ve done it, dear reader. I’ve braved the unknown, and unlike many… I’ve spoken to the Free Listening Guy. I was having a particularly rough week one day a couple years ago (probably, quite frankly, Sophomore Year, when everything was terrible) on which I checked out a BlueBike in front of Maseeh Hall and was riding along up Mass Ave when I found myself in the earlier described scene: a nice Cambridge evening passing in front of Lobby 7 and seeing that mysterious man and his mysterious sign reading his (arguably less) mysterious book. And, without anywhere else to turn to and nothing else to do, I whipped my bike around, parked it back at the stop, jogged back over to the intersection, and hesitantly… sat down next to him. I remember him looking up at me with a smile that felt familiar, warm. He closed his book gently, not as if he’d been interrupted but more like he’d been waiting to talk to someone–to talk to me. And then, he said… “Hello.” “Uh. Hi. I’m Caleb.” “Hi, Caleb. How are you doing?” And the rest just flowed out of me. I talked about school, about friends, about fitting in, about love, about everything under the sun and everything on my shoulders. I talked and I talked and I talked, finally feeling like there was somewhere to put everything that had been weighing on me–not to offload it, but at least to realize, to bring into order, to serialize. And, as the sign said, he listened. He listened intently to everything I had to share. He listened without interrupting, internalizing each monologue I jumped through. He listened carefully, quietly, inquisitively. And then, contrary to popular belief… he responded. He asked me about each of the things I told him. He helped me parse my thoughts, understand what I was feeling a little better, understand why I felt how I did. We back-and-forthed about everything I was going through, and the knotted mess of what I was dealing with that week slowly started to untangle. A few people passed in front of us. Some stopped and stared from afar. Some came a little closer, trying to eavesdrop on our conversation. I remember the only time he stopped me was to say, “Wait-… Hello,” to tell those trying to glean something from what we were talking about, broach the mystery of the Free Listening Guy, that this was unfortunately not a conversation that they were privy to. I appreciated him guarding my privacy and looking out for me in that moment of vulnerability. The conversation went on, and the world got darker and darker as the sun dredged further and further from the horizon and the evening continued. But he never told me to stop, or that he had to leave, or that we had been talking for too long. We could’ve been there for 20 minutes or an hour, but it was okay–it felt like I’d found a safe harbor to rest from the battering winds of life. Finally, I felt seen. By this man I’d never spoken a word to before, who knew nothing of me besides what I’d just shared, I felt understood. He’s got a knack for understanding. Eventually, the discussion started to lead toward a closing point, at which he made one request of me. “I want you to close your eyes.” I obliged. “And I want you to imagine…” In the next few minutes, he painted me a vibrant scene of my own life. I can’t pin down all the particular details, as this was quite a long time ago, but I believe that it was something along the lines of my life some years down the road, looking back on this moment when I’ve overcome these stressors and issues and my life has settled into its form and I felt accepted wherever I walked. I don’t remember it completely, but I do remember the vividity of the image he built against the dark black of my inner eyelids, and I remember the warm rivulets of catharsis rolling down my cheeks as I listened, soaking in the scene like lifeblood. After opening my eyes and wiping my cheeks, I thanked him profusely, stood up, and went back to the BlueBike stop. As it turned out, I had left my keys in the checkout slot in the bike dock when I had checked one out before sitting down, and they would’ve probably been completely lost had I not turned back to talk to the guy with the sign. I’m not very strongly spiritual, but that seemed like a very powerful coincidence–this conversation helped me find the keys to getting back home. Interesting indeed. I spoke to The Free Listening Guy every time I saw him from then on. If he was in conversation, I would just say hello and keep walking so that the person he was chatting with could retain the same privacy that he held in such importance during our first talk. But if he’s just reading, as he often is, I’ll sit down, this time without hesitating, and say “Hey!” And he’ll always say, “Hello, Caleb. How are you?” And we’ll sit around and chat, catching up from the last time that he was randomly generated in front of Lobby 7 at the same time that I was passing by and had the time to sit. Exactly a year ago today, I came to him with some more thoughts–I was turning 20 in just over a week, and I was scared about letting my youth go and getting old and all of the things that I’m always talking about. And as always, he listened, and then he responded. But this time, as we got further in the conversation, we turned the premise on its head. I wanted to give him some of the kindness he’d shown me and so many other people in their adventures through MIT and the wider world. So, that night (which I actually believe was only a few days after Kindness Friday), I asked him more about himself, how he was doing, how life was situated around him. And, just as I had opened up to him, he opened up to me. He trusted me to listen, and I did the best I could. I might not have been as elegant in my responses, but I lent my ear, and for that night, I was his Free Listening Guy. The Free Listening Guy has supported me in some really challenging moments in my time at MIT, showing up like a guardian to help me push through whatever might be weighing me down. But, more than that, he inspired me to be a better listener myself. And I think that’s part of his whole mission, right? To get us to listen to each other more. I think it’s abundantly obvious that we don’t listen to each other enough these days. Our lives move so fast these days that we don’t dedicate enough time to just listening to each other. But that act is one of the most foundational aspects of being a social being. We have to share the pieces ourselves with others, and we have to accept that which the people we care about share with us. That’s the best way that I can define being there for each other. If you find yourself one day feeling lost or confused or if you just need to disentangle the mess of thoughts you’re trapped in, turn to someone who cares about you, and share. Because to care about somebody, to be there for them, is to listen when you need them. Don’t keep things that you’re worried about or afraid of locked up in your own mind–instead, lean on the people you love and let them hold you up. Work through the things you’re afraid of, and let your community be your lantern through the inky dark. And, on the other side, be there for people. When people turn to you, listen. That’s one of the deepest acts of love we have. Make space for them to be understood, and do your best to understand. Be comfortable with the uncomfortable and the painful. Lift the weight off of the shoulders of the people you care about, or at least help them hold it for a few minutes. Listen without judgement. Listen kindly. Listen freely. The Free Listening Guy is, I would argue, one of the most important icons of daily life at MIT. He cares so deeply about people, people he doesn’t know, and you can feel it in every word he shares. If you see him sitting there one day, I encourage you to go up to him and say hello, even if you don’t have something difficult to work through. Just talk, and just listen. He’s one of the kindest people I’ve met here in Cambridge, if not in my nearly 21 years of living, and the conversations we’ve had have had a significant impact on my life, my time in college, and the way I view the world. Knowing him has made me kinder, stronger, more open, more honest, more ready to support the people that I care about. And I think it could do the same for anyone–as long as they’re willing to talk. Now, you might be wondering–Caleb, if you’ve spoken to this guy so many times, why do you keep calling him the Free Listening Guy? What’s his name? Well, I do know, yeah. It’s really not a mystery. But I won’t tell you–what’s the fun in that? Instead, next time it’s a sunny day in Cambridge and the sky is clear and you glance down to the corner of the steps and see a very particular man sitting there, walk over. Sit down, say hello, and talk a bit. Tell him about your life, your dreams, your worries. Know him as a person, and let him know you as one too. Ask… …and, freely, listen.

Title: The Sophomore Slump
Author: Nicholas R. '29
Article Content: I find “sophomore slump” to be quite the interesting term. For one, it gets thrown around in a lot of different contexts—from music and visual media to sports and, of course, academics. I’ve always wondered how this phenomenon, which sounds fairly specific, pervades such a variety of spaces. Just over a month in to my sophomore year, I’m starting to understand (and, crucially, experience) how it does at MIT. A couple obvious culprits to point out: there’s no longer the cushion of P/NR and ABC/NR,⁠01First-years have a unique grading system. During fall semester, classes are graded on a Pass/No Record basis: a passing grade of C- or above will show up as 'P' on a transcript, while a failing grade won't show up at all. During spring semester, letter grades are given for any passed classes, but the No Record policy still applies. a true blessing for frosh. Additionally, most sophomores begin transitioning from the GIRs⁠02General Institute Requirements and other introductory courses to major-specific, often harder, courses. While I’d say that my classes this semester are harder than last spring, I feel like the comparison is heightened because I never really found proper footing. The start of this school year felt like a blur, driven by the hecticness of Orientation and, much more so, Rush week⁠03Rush is the week after first-year orientation, when all of the frats and sororities host recruitment events for students interested in joining Greek life . (I got sick during Rush, which didn’t help either). Classes started somewhere amidst that blur and I found myself swept in its current, already fatigued, unable to take a breath. All of this to say, the first month has been a bit rough for me. I’ve been feeling caught in a vicious cycle of falling behind in a class, slacking off in my other classes to catch up, then falling behind in those other classes as a result. In the last two weeks I got hit with my first wave of midterms, though I’m not sure that really even describes it. More accurately, I got smacked upside the head by my first tsunami of midterms. My own academic turmoil aside, I’ve found my classes to be very interesting overall. Here’s a brief overview of what I’m taking this semester, supplemented with some of my notes from lectures: 18.03 – Differential Equations As a corequisite to 10.10, I have to take this class. While my relationship with math in general is very love-hate (in the case of last fall’s 18.02,⁠04Multivariable Calculus mostly hate), I’m enjoying 18.03 a lot more than I anticipated. The lectures are great. It’s also very applicable: I’ve noticed a lot of conceptual overlap between this class, classes I’m taking, and classes I’ve already taken here. I guess this makes sense, since differential equations are used to model natural laws and systems. An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next This was the first of my midterms. Though I didn’t do as well as I’d hoped, I’m not too upset or stressed because we get a drop exam for the class. If anything, it’s a much-needed motivator for me to be extra prepared for the next exam. I also feel like I’m getting a better grip on the material as the current topics are reinforcing previous ones. 5.601 – Thermodynamics Sigh. I did really bad on the first midterm for this class. Like almost-two-standard-deviations-below-the-average bad. This especially sucks because 5.601 is a half-semester subject, so there are only two exams for the class, each one being worth 40% of our grade. I think my performance was a result of my general fuzziness on some topics, multiplied by my tendency to cram-study practice problems. An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next So far we’ve covered the first three laws of thermodynamics (i.e., the zeroth, first, and second laws). Between those three, I find the second law to be coolest to think about: while the first law simply states that the energy of the universe is conserved, the second law describes the directionality of time; specifically, how the entropy of the universe always increases over time. You may be familiar with the idea of entropy as “disorder,” but “order” is a pretty subjective metric. According to my professor, it can be more accurately thought of as the number of microscopic configurations (“microstates”) of a system. In reality, this often manifests as something ostensibly more “chaotic” or “disordered,” but not always. There’s definitely a metaphor in here somewhere for how my life feels at the moment, but I digress. 10.10 – Introduction to Chemical Engineering For the introductory class to my major, this class hasn’t gripped me very much. It’s not that it’s boring, but rather tedious. We spent the first month learning mass and energy balances of chemical systems. One of my gripes (besides the confusing notation) is that the majority of lecture time is spent doing nitty-gritty calculations for example problems, rather than building up our problem-solving intuition. It feels like I’m scrambling to copy down what the professor writes on the board, while retaining very little about how to actually approach problems on a higher, more conceptual level. An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Now, we’ve switched to the Python portion of the class—we’re using it to solve system balances that would be otherwise impossible to do by hand. I enjoy coding, so I’m hoping that I’ll start enjoying this class more. (Just as I finished writing this, I got my first midterm grade back. Surprise! Another subpar performance, but not nearly as bad as 5.601, thankfully). 6.1010 – Fundamentals of Programming Speaking of coding, I’m also taking 6.1010! The previous three classes I’ve discussed are standard for a sophomore course 10/10B⁠05Chemical Engineering/Biological-Chemical Engineering schedule. This one is less so. For some context, I came into MIT with zero programming experience. After taking and loving 6.100A⁠06Introduction to CS and Programming using Python last fall, I decided that I wanted to explore more computer science classes (with the goal of pursuing a minor in course 6⁠07Electrical Engineering and Computer Science or possibly a double-major with 6-7,⁠08Computer Science and Molecular Biology if I’m feeling really masochistic ambitious). The weekly coding assignments for this class are super cool. This past week focused on using recursion to implement an autocomplete engine. The week prior I built a working solver for the puzzle game Snekoban! These assignments have been really helpful in honing the basics that I learned last year to build more fully-fledged projects. I also enjoy the structure of the class, with asynchronous readings and built-in software labs every Tuesday to help get progress on that week’s assignment, which is due on Friday; it makes tackling the assignment a lot less intimidating, and also forces me to not procrastinate. CMS.306 – Making Comics and Sequential Art This one’s probably my favorite. While it’s been on my radar, I wasn’t planning to take it this semester. After not getting into either CI-H⁠09A CI-H is a Communication-Intensive course in the Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences. It's part of the GIRs I’d preregistered for, I decided to add it. It’s a 7-10 PM class on Wednesday nights, which might sound awful but it’s not. This is helped by the fact that we do a lot of in-class drawing exercises, during which Professor Jason Wiser lectures about topics relevant to the art of comic-making. I will say that it’s quite a lot of work, especially for a HASS⁠10Humanites, Arts, and Social Sciences class (which, from my experience, usually demand less time outside of class than technicals⁠11Non-HASS (i.e. STEM) classes ). Still, I find this work to be very satisfying. An instructional comic, for one of our homework assignments. An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Right now, we’ve started to work on our final, which has two components: a personal creative comic along with a science research comic. The latter is a group project made in collaboration with the MIT Museum for an upcoming summer exhibition. I will definitely dedicate a future blog (or blogs) to this class, because it really is that awesome. A drawing exercise from class: the prompt was to draw any building, then draw an evil version of it! So that’s my semester so far, in a nutshell. I’m torn between feelings of disappointment in myself, knowing I can do better, but I’m also trying to give myself grace. Truthfully, I wish I could hit rewind on the semester, but because this would violate the second law of thermodynamics, I have to move forward (and, hopefully, upwards!) I’m trying my best to stay motivated and not let this slump get the best of me. When I’m at a low point like this, I have to remind myself that there’s really no other place I’d rather be struggling academically.

Title: b.i.r.t.h.f.d.a.y.c.a.k.e
Author: Emily P. '28
Article Content: Two of my lovely friends, Tina and Brandon, have the same birthday: October 5th. It’s always a fabulous time; I say time and not day because we don’t always celebrate it on the 5th, but we have celebrated it in some way or another for the past 3 years. This year, Hannah and I were tasked with the weighty responsibility of baking the cake for a little gathering they planned to host at Tina’s apartment. As two Mince members,⁠01obligatory Mince mentionwe wanted the cake to be yummy, beautiful, and just straight-up awesome. How hard can that be? Or rather, how long could that possibly take? Hannah and I requesting cake flavor preferences wednesday afternoon / night Tuesday night, Hannah and I had browsed a bunch of cake recipes and had a shopping list in mind. A very small shopping list, because I, with an abysmal amount of confidence, said, “Yeah, I have like, almost everything.” And so we saunter off to the Whole Foods in Central Square to purchase a can of very much overpriced Dutch processed cocoa powder, some 70% dark chocolate bars, and a bottle of molasses.⁠02Adam Ragusea (another obligatory mention) has a whole thing about not buying brown sugar because brown sugar is just white sugar plus molasses and brown sugar always clumps up so you’re better off buying white sugar and adding molasses whenever you need brown sugarBecause that’s all we need. Because I already have everything else. Afterwards, we make our way over to the basement of Walker Memorial because Hannah, along with Carter and birthday girl Tina, have a radio show together! Called Codependent, they’ve been on air every semester since freshman fall (it was started with Linda, another really close friend of ours). And despite being friends with many-a-WMBR members, it was my first time down in the station. Sniped everyone I knew on the photowall, including fellow blogger Caleb M. '27! I’m struggling to articulate the awesome vibe you get when you’re down there – it’s one of those spaces you have to be physically present in to get it. The incredible record library, the slightly musty but cozy basement yellow lighting, the studios packed with cool and old looking hardware, the funky experimental tracks on air you can’t help but Shazam… point is, you should go listen to WMBR @ 88.1FM! We trek back to Burton Conner after the show; it’s finally time to bake some cake. Hannah starts the cherry compote while I continue to mull over which chocolate cake recipe to follow. As I’m eyeing the different ingredients lists, it dawns on me that, uh oh, I don’t have enough eggs. Uh oh x2, I don’t have any coffee or espresso either! Luckily, B1 has an “items-request” text channel: ignore my username. And so I run off to the 141, where Emma asks the dreaded question, “how many eggs do you need?” Hannah and I had decided on this serious eats recipe by Stella Parks, and because it churns out three 8” round cakes, it calls for a grand total of 9 eggs. I happened to only have 2. “Could I get 7 eggs?” Yeah, no, that’s kind of a ridiculous ask. But as it just so happens, John, who’s another fellow Mince member, is also in the suite, listening in on my crazy request. We make eye contact. Woah. Flashbacks to New House Country Kitchen, fridge closest to the entrance, where there’s just a whole door rack filled with eggs.⁠03from a recent Mince pop-up. I was not stealing some unlucky New House resident’s eggs! “John, are there still eggs in New House?” John is thinking the exact same thing. John is awesome. “Yeah, there’s so many. I can go grab some?” I thank John profusely (but his kindness can not possibly be repaid in words) and run back to my suite to finally start working on the cakes. John delivers not 9, but 10 whole ass eggs. Just in case there was a bad egg in there! Whilst I’m chopping the chocolate, Ronnie⁠04that’s Veronica P. '27 for those who don't knowruns out of her room and out the suite, yelling something about “TV lounge” and “pastries.” Oh shit! I also book it out of the suite and down the side stairwell, listening to the booming thumps of other like-minded students sprinting down the stairs from above. The door swings open to heaven, pretty much: Japonaise bakery pastry spread Carolina, a grad student and friend of floor, is also friends with the owner of Japonaise Bakery in Brookline. Pastries that are past their prime and would normally be thrown away are donated to food shelters, or, if they’re really scuffed, brought to the perpetually pastry-hungry residents of Burton Conner. And so about once a week, Carolina pulls up to Burton Conner with a giant sack of treats⁠05she’s kind of like Santa Claus now that I think about it, and Christmas is every Tuesday like 9pm ish.in her car. A bc-talk email is sent out, and a stampede ensues. I shove a scrumptious chikuwa pan in my mouth and hurry back to the cake baking. This Stella Parks recipe was particularly fun, as everything gets mixed in one giant pot and it’s kind of witchy in that way. She even includes how much batter by weight goes into each pan.⁠06this is the level of precision instructional writing I aspire forOnce divided evenly, the cakes went into the oven at 350° for about 30 minutes. butter in very witchy large pot hannah chops chocolate cakes bout to bake An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Now, Hannah and I mull over the rest of the cake. The compote had reduced quite a bit, to the point where it looked like I would have to buy more cherries the next day. Furthermore, we envisioned the final cake to be this intense, slate-colored, smooth, minimalistic cylinder with broody deep-purple / almost-black flowers to match. Issue is, we initially planned to frost it with whipped ganache, which would definitely give us the color we wanted. Oh, and also, we have no heavy whipping cream, which is one of two ganache ingredients. … “Yeah, I have like, almost everything.” Long story short, John comes to the rescue once again, and Joanne⁠07another Mince member, who was also head chef of last year's cake picnic!!assists in making this incredible chocolate buttercream, featuring another Stella Parks recipe. the yummiest chocolate buttercream, ft. Joanne leveled cake Hannah patches up a giant hole, whoops An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next We finish the core components around 1:30 am. Hannah and I stay up to chat just a little longer, despite both having gotten minimal schoolwork done and needing to wake up early the next morning. Neither of us seem that stressed. We’re content, even. thursday afternoon / night We frost the cake with the much appreciated assistance / supervision of Joanne. cleaning up cardboard base The ‘party’ was scheduled for 8:30, and given we still needed to buy flowers, we hurried over around 7:30. It was my first time at Tina’s apartment this year, and it was so cozy! After we dropped off the cake, we walked to Fern, picked out the aforementioned broody deep-purple / almost-black flowers, and stopped by Whole Foods (again…) for candles. … “Yeah, I have like, almost everything.” giant freaking cake, old ah elevator oh my god Tina and Brandon!!!! gorgeous flowers at Fern An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next By the time we make it back to the apartment, the rest of the guests have arrived. Title: Note-Taking in its Many Forms
Author: Sara N. '28
Article Content: I have always love taking notes. In a sense, it’s for the same reason why I like to write. It anchors me when everything else is free and floating. More concretely: In lecture, my natural tendency is to disengage and become glassy-eyed as soon as I get lost; note-taking reminds me to continue to listen and to just write down what I see and hear, even when (especially when!) nothing is making sense. On days when I’m running on too-little sleep, the friction and rhythm of pencil on paper helps me keep my eyes open. Note-taking helps me detangle concepts: I’ve long believed that if I can make something clear on paper, then it can become clear in my mind. It calms me down. When I feel hopelessly behind in a class, note-taking is a clear, immediately actionable step I can take to regain footing. Outside of working through practice problems and exams, note-taking (not note-reviewing) is the primary way I study for exams. In fact, beyond occasionally looking back to see how I’ve solved a problem in the past, I rarely look back on my notes. Almost all of my exam studying consists of writing new notes from scratch. I often end up taking notes on the same content three different times at varying levels of detail: once in real-time, during lecture, where I write down whatever I can catch; once more after lecture, slower and more exact as I takes notes off a lecture recording or associated reading; and a final time as I distill the big ideas to get ready for an exam. Here is what my notes look like, in all their many forms: (from 9.40 -- Introduction to Neural Computation) this class was so incredibly interesting -- it was my first time seeing differential equations, probability theory, and circuit theory being applied to neuroscience. I came into 6.310 never having heard of control theory, and left thinking it was some of the most interesting math I’ve ever come across. Title: i miss home
Author: Hala K. '29
Article Content: I took my first exam last week. And in my two semesters’ worth of experience, the first exam marks the start of the end. Prior to the first exam: You only have psets to worry about – which in and of itself is a lot but not nearly as stressful as finishing psets AND studying for an exam. The content hasn’t completely built on itself yet so if lecture 2 doesn’t make sense, you can probably still piece together what lecture 3 is about. You don’t actually know how you are doing in any of your classes. You can convince yourself that even though none of the content makes sense to you – you will pull the biggest lock in of all time and somehow, the exams will feel light. You don’t think about your final grade nearly as much. You are missing too many important numbers to actually know what you’d get if you got X score on the final. However, once the first exam passes, all of these statements become false. It seems like the exams will NEVER end. One week is 6.1910 and the next is 2.001 and 6.1210 ON THE SAME DAY. (Can you tell this isn’t a hypothetical?) my friend from home texting me about reading over her college apps i had to be honest... "this week" has just ended for context - next is much worse. don't worry though we worked out times - she has me "booked" for October 19th and on An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next And to make matters worse, while you were studying for exam #1, you probably said “well I’m going to focus on ___ class for this week and will just catch up on the rest next week, post-exam.” However, there is a fundamental flaw in this plan because post-exam #1 = pre-exam #2 – so how will you catch up when you need to study for exam #2. Something has got to give – and it usually comes down to sleep or your willingness to leave an assignment unsubmitted. And the cycle repeats, over and over again, until the semester finishes, And then starts all over again the next semester. It’s incredibly draining – you’re tired, studying constantly, looking at exam scores and being disappointed that you didn’t do quite as good as you wanted to, trying to find time to see people so you don’t completely hole yourself up in your room. Though what makes this harder, is that these feelings are directly proportional to feelings of homesickness. Specifically, as the year goes on, you are getting more tired at the same rate that you are feeling more and more homesick. You are realizing that this is no longer some “temporary” place that you are visiting but instead, it’s your new normal. You miss the support systems that were already built up for you at home. You miss your dad bringing tangerines and the crunchiest green grapes for you to snack on as you work. You miss those super-tight hugs your mom gives you when you’re stressed, or her barging into your room to distract you with funny stories about her students. You really really really miss the delicious Lebanese food your mom cooks (you genuinely dream of warak enab and mloukhieh). You miss just being in your house – sleeping in your comfy bed, studying in the best desk chair, hearing your sisters arguing in the room beside you, helping your mom grade some papers while you pick up a new tv show together. You miss your friends – the drives with olivia rodrigo blasting, the late night blizzard⁠01as in the dairy queen ones, not the weather ones runs, laughing about the same inside joke you probably laughed at the day before but somehow doesn’t seem to get any less funny. You miss having hobbies – reading in your backyard with your huge tree shielding you from the sun, binge watching sitcoms, learning a new variant of sudoku, and most importantly, just laying down doing absolutely nothing. You miss home. And if this blog didn’t already make it incredibly clear – “you” is me. I miss home. A lot. But a lot of people I’ve spoken to recently have shared similar sentiments. We miss home. The issue is that I unfortunately don’t have a solution for this. It’s a pretty sad way to end the blog but I have too many complicated and conflicting thoughts on this topic that seem to change every day. I think that it’s normal to genuinely love where you are while desperately missing where you were before. I think I’m starting to get how IHTFP. Though, one note on this is that my homesickness differs significantly from how it felt freshman year. After spending a whole year saying “all I want to do is go home,” when I was home this summer, there were a couple moments where I thought to myself: I kind of want to be back at MIT right now. I have “real” friends here now. I no longer consider them “MIT friends” who are distinct from those back home but actual ones that I genuinely love so so so much (sorry to my friends if you are reading this and realize that you must have hit a promotion at some point in the past year). I’m always excited for dinner to finally see them again and catch up on the inevitably embarrassing things that happened to us that day. I’m comfortable ranting to them about all of my stresses and admitting when I feel like I suck at MITing. They make me laugh until my stomach hurts and make me lose The Game almost every day (i don’t know if this is a niche pull). Maybe the real treasure was the friends we made along the way. Anyways… potentially more helpful, I wanted to share the playlist I made last year that I usually listen to when the homesickness seems to take over. Fair warning: I don’t believe in playlists making you feel better about something. Instead, I think they should actually make you feel worse. More specifically, I listen to a lot of sad music, so my playlists tend to reflect that.

Title: Obligatory Spider-Man Post
Author: Kayode D. '27
Article Content: [this blog is so so late, but it’s about the goat and i need to post it, so here it is!!:] Last night, I went with some friends to watch Spider-Man Brand New Day at the movie theater. I LOVED IT. I think it’s the best on yet, and my favorite movie of the year hands down. I’ve been thinking about going back to watch it again tonight… I was telling my mom about it, and she said I should make a blog pointing out the MIT references the movie had, and there were a good few!! Light spoilers ahead and heavy spoilers at the end of this blog. MIT References [Light Spoilers] In Spider-Man No Way Home, Ned and MJ get accepted to MIT in the class of 2028. Spider-Man does not get to go because of space-time hijinx, and spends the next 4 years watching them enjoy MIT through Ned’s social media. We don’t get to see much of MIT⁠01no scenes were shot at MIT from what I could tell , as all we get is a montage of the years passing. There is one notable exception. Towards the end of their time at MIT, Ned says the line: “Final Semester at MIT! Oh, my gosh we’re graduating in a month. We’ve made so many memories. Where do I begin? Night swimming in the Charles River with Jim and Wiley. The infamous food fight at the banana lounge. Pulling all-nighters at Stud 5 with MJ and Nate Dawg. It seems like yesterday I was sitting on a roof with MJ…” So much to unpack here. Let’s break it down: Night Swimming in the Charles River: Very much not recommended. The Charles river is not clean enough to swim in, especially not at night. I know someone who was doing a research study on the bacteria growing in the river…all I’m saying is that this one isn’t a flex. Infamous Food Fight at the Banana Lounge: The Banana Lounge is a space on campus where large crates of bananas are regularly delivered. There is definitely the ammo for this, but the space is pretty tight to constitute a full on food fight. It would be very notable, though. Pulling all nighters at Stud 5: This one had us losing our minds. This is elite ball knowledge. The other two you could make up with some google searches but to know about stud 5?? Stud 5 is the fifth floor of the Student Center, a big study space where students often pull all nighters, especially during the end of the semesters.⁠02My friends and I have spent many nights there… but for them to mention this in the movie?? ELITE Ball knowledge. I wonder who they talked to to get that line. Has to have been a student or someone. Hmmmm… Other than that, there isn’t much else mentioned about MIT in the movie. There is one other thing I took note on: At one part, MJ tells Peter that before she switched to studying Aero-astro, she wanted to study Biochemical Engineering. She then looks at his device and solves an issue. While walking home after the movie, I realized that there are very few [if any at all] classes that overlap in these two majors. To switch from course 10B to 16 would be a full academic career pivot, and one she would have to take before her sophomore year in order to take Unified, a series of Aero-Astro classes that most course 16’s take their sophomore year. So this means she only got at most a year of focused Biochemical engineering courses, which I’d wager isn’t enough to make the jumps and problem solving required to repair Peter’s tech. Unless she ASE’d out of all of her GIRs and did a full year of advanced biochemistry, and then FULL PIVOTED out of that into Aero-Astro…which is possible…or she did UROPs and independent research in that area while studying course 16…or if this is a superhero movie that I am overanalyzing in the nerdiest way possible. Also, no one was wearing their brass rats. Which is fair, people don’t wear them all the time, but still. Ok, MIT nerd nitpicking over. ABSOLUTE CINEMA This movie was SO PEAK. From Beginning to END!!! I think that this was the best superhero movie that I have seen…possibly ever. I felt like a kid again!! Watching Spidey beat the bad guys! And I like how they handled the power-creep this time around. We just finished arcs where Spider-Man was battling Thanos. It’s hard to make Batroc the Leaper feel like a gratifying next villain after the last one almost destroyed the planet. But they did it! A street-level Spider-man. Who woulda thunk? And the whole arc with MJ??? So many layers to it, such a good movie. Also, I LOVE THE MOVIES!! What?? I forgot how much fun the movies are. We went to the AMC in Boston Commons, near downtown. It was BUSTLING with people–mainly teens and college students– and it was a really fun time. In high school I worked at a pizza place, but if I ever left that job I wanted to work at the movie theater. I need to go back ASAP. Lowkey, I started this blog in July and didn’t finish it. Now I did, but I forget most of what I thought about this movie other than it’s good. I’d watch it again. Maybe I will and then I can make more comments on why it’s good. Happy Birthday, Maynard!

Title: bringing my digicam to class for a “week”
Author: Veronica P. '27
Article Content: Hi blog, I am an avid user of what kids these days are calling a digi— those digital cameras from the 2000’s that fit in your pocket, can document the date in the bottom right corner, and have a somewhat-unreliable flash system. 01I currently use the Canon Powershot ELPH, but I also really love the Sony Cybershot I think a big part of the appeal is the nostalgia— the photos look like the ones you covet of your parents before you came around, when they were young and fun and carefree. As college students, now is our prescribed time to be young, fun and carefree. What better way to document it than with a digi?! Now, despite being my inspiration, my parents absolutely cannot get behind this. Isn’t the whole point of a phone that you have all of these devices in one? 02My roommate got me an iPod for my most recent birthday, only exacerbating their pain even more Why do you keep spending so much money on old things? 03They've essentially given up at this point on the thrifting front And, admittedly, I have blown through about 3 E-bay cameras in my time, but I have absolutely no regrets! My phone is an exhausting, anxiety-inducing time-suck at least half of the time. The more I can do to reduce my dependence on that rectangular prism, the better. As for the ‘old’ stuff: it’s taking up space in this world anyways, why not give it a new life? 04Let's call it 'pre-loved' However, I’ve come upon a recent dilemma with my digi usage. This whole young, fun, and carefree expectation I’ve put around it has made it such that my camera only really gets its mileage at 10 PM on a Friday. Or when I’m on vacation. These photos are great, but as a senior who is hyper-aware of her senior-ness I find that I want to capture every aspect of my life at MIT, not just the weekends. So, I set out to bring my digi-cam everywhere for a whole week of school. Let’s see how it went. monday a morning view of my suite! my roommate and i both ate breakfast on our desks. at 11:30, i hop onto a zoom to meet with the teaching team for 2.006, the course i TA, and eat leftover free thai food for lunch i have 2.009 (Product Engineering Processes) lecture and lab from 1-5pm, and this week we chose officer roles. i'm a system integrator, whose job is to coordinate amongst all of our subteams/task forces, plan lab agendas, keep our timeline on track, and help each of our subassemblies combine into a larger product. i forget to bring my digi out until the evening, when i'm prepping to hold office hours. two of my friends from floor are regular attendees! back in the suite, Emily P. '28 endeavors to make a loaf of banana bread for the floor. everyone is very happy!!! monday, again? After this first semi-successful day, I completely forgot to bring my camera around for the rest of the week. So, I present to you: more Monday. I wore the same outfit, totally for continuity and not by accident at all… good morning, ft. my roommate's unique seating choices my walk to the (newly opened) met warehouse a quick look inside as i get a latte from the cafe on the first floor. i take my teaching team meeting at some tables by the entrance and do some research on fellowships. a shot of 2.009 lecture before it's time to head into pappalardo lab! my team selected our final product concept today, which was a very long discussion. i'll leave more details about this product for a later blog! i come home to a few floor members doing work together! i hang out, eat dinner, and chat before i head out to office hours. tuesday… Not for lack of remembering, I chose not to document my Tuesday this week. After office hours on Monday, I started to do work grad school applications and, realizing just how real and imminent they were, began to feel incredibly overwhelmed and out of my depth. It was a rough night, and I felt even worse the next morning. In the afternoon, I had my weekly meeting with the grad student who supervises my UROP. I expressed a few of these feelings, and she was sweet enough to dedicate the hour to giving me guidance and support I needed to get back on track. Perhaps a blog for another time! I called my dad to update him on my talk, spent some time with my friend in Hayden, and then headed to a Mech-E grad school info session, motivation renewed. wednesday In the morning, I showed up to the booths in Lobby 10 to help Camp Kesem (also a blog for another time) promote their application cycle! I got free coffee and was able to catch up with a few counselors. I then went to Barker to send out a few grad-application emails I had been putting off, and then spent some time in Pappalardo preparing for the 2.009 build challenge on Friday (many, many photos to come). In the evening, I had System Integrator training for 2.009. Having lost my momentum, I didn’t document much. I did manage to get one photo, though… the bloggers!!! wrapping up our biweekly blog meeting. ft. many masks because freshman flu is real… thursday Okay, wow, I’m bad at this. I had a wave demo lab for 2.016 (Hydrodynamics) and drawing for designers class. friday BUILD CHALLENGE DAY!!! All of the 2.009 teams gather onto Killian Court to compete on a challenge course using cardboard devices. These devices had to move our teams payload (puzzle pieces) 16′ at a time as quickly as possible, without leaving the loading/unloading zones. We were given the following materials: cardboard, paper tape, wooden dowels, cotton robe, and two-five gallon buckets of water. Our two devices had the following unique requirements: Device 1: Can only touch the group in loading/unloading zones and a 3′ x 3′ box on the ground in the middle. This ended up being our school bus! device 1: one long rope remains in tension to hang the device above the ground, while two ropes on either side can be pulled to move the device towards the loading/unloading zones! Device 2: Can only have one actuated rotational degree of freedom. This was our Lightning McQueen!. our device 2, lightning mcqueen! we used ropes to spin the axle of the front and back wheels. However, the prize isn’t actually for moving the most puzzle pieces the fastest, it’s for team spirit! So, here’s some photos of Red Team on the competition course, featuring my teammate’s digi as well! red team on the course!!!! we ended up finishing first, and blue team won the prize for team spirit! And there we have it! Sort of a week in my life, through my digi lens. Everyone knows that social media only captures the highs, but I really underestimated how difficult it would be for me to photograph the lows and the room-temperatures of the week. I’d love to attempt this again, with more than 3 days to show for myself. For now, however, I’m glad to have these snapshots to look back on, and remember when I was young, selectively fun, and definitely not carefree.

a 6 major like a Lot of people at mit. it is just not something that appeals to me. people told me to be a 6-7⁠01aka majoring in computational biology(ha ha six seven)⁠02for those not reading this in
