nothing february 2025: nothing march 2025: nothing april 2025: nothing may 2025: nothing june 2025: nothing july 2025: nothing august 2025: nothing september 2025: nothing october 2025: nothing november 2025: nothing december 2025: nothing january 2026: nothing february 2026: nothing march 2026: nothing april 2026: nothing may 2026: nothing june 2026: nothing july and august 2026: i decide to try to ase⁠06advanced standing exams - basically lets you skip some classes if you pass the corresponding test; exists because mit doesn’t really accept ap exams out of 6.100A, which means i have to relearn everything that i forgot over the past year and a half. what this boiled down to is i went through the sample exam that they gave us, solving the “write code!” problems and thinking about the multiple choice. i realized that even though i’d forgotten a lot of the syntax, i still remembered a lot of the like thought processes and approaches that are often helpful when programming.⁠07for example insert print statements everywhere when your crap don’t workg also i did some of “watch people who are better than me code” which was maybe helpful. not sure. october 2026 (now): i finally do something that’s not “speedrun a class” or “take a test” with coding. whaaaaat so what am i doing? this semester i’m taking a class called 12.004, aka intro to the global carbon cycle. it’s in the earth, atmospheric, and planetary sciences department as one of their 4 intro classes. this class is about all the places that carbon is sequestered and how it moves around, especially in the ocean⁠08one of the instructors is an oceanographer by training which basically means that it is a class that i think is awesome, because i really like the ocean and i want to work on climate and the carbon cycle is AAAAAA so important. this class is interesting because it combines typical lecture about like theory (right now a lot of chemistry) with a significant computational portion. to illustrate, this week we’ve been working on a pset that has two parts. part one is the theoretical part: one question asks us to “Determine what fraction of nitrogen (N2) is in the atmosphere vs. the ocean,” while the other has us derive an expression for the dissolved oxygen concentration in a hypothetical raindrop over time. this part was deceptively hard for me, but i went to office hours with the professor and then everything made sense! so yay part two is the computational part. basically we are writing some code to do some annoying arithmetic for us as we develop “box models”. what do i mean by a box model? well, here’s a drawing from my notes: yeah there are more detailed ones but i realized i didn’t copy them down but you just abstract different things down to little boxes that interact with each other in simple ways. our first coding project is a two-box model: there is the atmosphere, which has co2, and the ocean, which has dissolved co2, which then reacts with water to form bicarbonate and a proton, and then the bicarb disassociates to form carbonate and another proton. we introduce a bunch of different constraints and eventually end up with a system of 7 equations and 7 unknowns, which we want to solve. the coding part of this is really not intense – or perhaps it is more accurate to say that it isn’t really the focus of the problem solving ?? i looked at the pset before we talked about it in class, and i was confused as to how we were supposed to code something that generated a polynomial in H+ concentration. it turns out we just do that part by hand and end up with a cubic in H+ that we can then solve and then replug into everything else. but we do code a simple root-finder! yippee. back to what the pset wants me to do! part 1 asked us to complete the work we’d done in class by fully finding dic (which stands for dissolved inorganic carbon – basically co2 + hco3- + (co3)2-) given the partial pressure of co2 in the atmosphere. yeah looking back at my code i am not a huge fan of the way i set this up but it’s probably fine??? this was reasonably straightforward i feel. parts 2, 3, and 4 asked me to generate some plots using matplotlib. this was the part that really shocked me – i had actually never used matplotlib ever and had some sort of innate fear of it.⁠09i would much rather use google sheets, or desmos, or just draw it by hand so it was pretty crazy when (after learning the syntax for how to plot a simple two-axis plot) my code just worked first try it and generated a REAL GRAPH. i was like wtf i texted both my friend scarlet and my little brother to be like holy crap i feel so powerful. this is also what pushed me to write this post! wow look at that plot! ignore the units part 5 was basically the same thing as part 1; just solve a slightly different cubic that is given to us and then plug and solve into the rest of the other equations. we also had to go back and make sure that this works by checking with our answers from part 1. part 6… part 6 stumped me for a while. it is a much different form of question than the other 5 parts: where the other 5 asked to plot or to implement a general solver, part 6 asked us to use the tools we previously came up with and make some assumptions in order to estimate the pco2 of a parcel of water gradually moving northward over the course of a month. what this ends up being like is asking us to make a very simple differential equation numerical solver; i lowkey don’t know if i could have come up with the actual differential equation⁠10which seems bad, like why am i taking 18.03 then in closed form but i feel like i did good enough. basically my workflow for solving this problem was stare at the question be confused stare harder try to think give up find a chalkboard draw on the chalkboard drawing on chalkboards is really fun. i think this might be a big reason why people decide to do math, just because drawing on chalkboards makes you feel intellectual. but chalkboard was good for writing down ideas! if anyone is working on this very pset rn don’t look at my work it is like a lot wrong the chalkboarding took place from like 9:30 to 10:30pm in a random classroom in building 66; then i went back to tetazoo and watched people play tomodachi life while i typed stuff up. while typing it up i realized that my first initial model made no sense – the answer i got was like lower than it started, when i felt like it should probably be higher. i went to my room because i was very sleepy; i then realized that the reason why my model didn’t make sense is that i didn’t realize that my code also calculated the value of a coefficient that i needed but didn’t know i had. then i went to sleep because it was like 2am i got to watch a wedding while i worked on my pset! so wholesome after i woke up i fixed my code and made some new assumptions, and i think it went well. my actual solution turned out much simpler than what i was initially cooking up; it did kind of feel like i wasted a lot of time thinking, but whatever! it’s fine. i turned in the pset a whole twelve hours before it was due (could have been better but this last problem was hard) and then stopped thinking about it. my final submitted pdf ended up being 8 pages and my code ended up being 223 lines long thoughts on coding i definitely am not the cleanest coder. for example, i think i am missing some modularity, because i have two basically identical functions that just find roots of slightly different functions, but the way i have them set up there’s something internal that’s different, so i just have two copies. with a bit of extra time i could probably make a general root-finder, but this is like not the point of this part of the class i think. i also think i am not particularly efficient? like not like my code is inefficient, I AM inefficient as i write my code. on the other hand i completely understand the satisfaction of having your code work. i kind of felt this while i was reviewing for the ase – it’s really satisfying to see the thing you typed up actually successfully do what it’s supposed to. but also i feel like i am just really not a good programmer and i don’t know if i want to put in the work to become a good programmer⁠11especially at this point in time… i know some people say that it is meaningless to learn how to code when LLMs are so good at it, but i feel like this is kinda cringe. let it be known that no LLMs were used in the course of this assignment (except for as a last resort when i was crashing out trying to find values of henry’s coefficient for co2 before realizing it is literally in the code) i did really enjoy this assignment tho! our final project in this class is like this but more detailed and Title: The Incorrect Biological Hypothesis
Author: Aiden H. '28
Article Content: A couple of week’s ago, MIT’s film/cinema club LSC⁠01Lecture Series Committee hosted a pre-screening of the new hit rom-com “The Love Hypothesis” in 26-100⁠02The largest lecture hall on campus. for free! I didn’t go (oops!), but I did watch the movie the night it came out on Prime Video.⁠03The worst streaming service. Off to a bad start... If you don’t know, the movie follows the fake-dating, enemies-to-lovers romance between a biology PhD student, Olive, and a biology post-doc, Adam. I think the reason it was chosen as one of MIT’s exclusive pre-screenings is because the movie is very science- and academia-focused. What a mistake! Showing a movie so deeply embedded in scientific practice to a group of scientists is a sure-fire way for the absolute most criticism. And oh my god were there so many errors. Most people talking about the movie are obviously not focused on correct biological practices and instead on the over-six-foot-totally-jacked-genius professor, but trust that I am holding the fort down. To get this off my chest, here is everything (that I can remember) that The Love Hypothesis gets wrong about biology/academia: 1. Olive’s Dorm Early in the movie, Olive is shown to have a very traditional, undergraduate-style dorm room. This is wrong for many reasons. Mostly that if Olive were to live in an undergraduate dorm, she would be an RA and would therefore have a much larger dorm with its own bathroom and kitchenette. However, most likely, Olive would have lived in a graduate dorm, which almost universally have apartment-style housing instead of individual dorm rooms. Eventually, Olive does move out with her friends into an off-campus house, which is more realistic. 2. Lab Bathroom A key scene at the beginning of the movie involves the two main characters meeting in what Adam calls his “lab bathroom”. This is not a thing. First, it is ridiculous to assume that any university has enough funding to have a full bathroom that is out of commission just to have extra lab sinks. Second, this is a total safety hazard to have an extraneous, publicly accessible location with exposure to any biologicals or chemicals. Like, you have to have gloves and all the safety signs and things. Third, most biologicals Adam would be using can’t be poured down a normal sink drain either, but in specialized lab sinks that are specifically hooked to different sewer lines so as to not create mass exposure to random things. 3. That’s not how a Post-Doc works One of the key differences between the book and the movie is that, in the book, Adam is a professor in the biology department, while in the movie he is only a post-doc. The reasoning behind this was to lessen the severity of the power-gap between the characters and reduce stigma. Unfortunately, they forgot to fix every other detail that involves the differences in power between a post-doc and professor. Essentially, the movie just treats Adam as a professor, and calls him a post-doc. He has his own office and laboratory and PhD students (fully not a thing, only professors have this–post-docs work in labs under professors instead). Also, he himself applies and renews his own grants, when again post-docs work under labs where the professor is the main point for funding. He also is the keynote speaker at a large biology conference later in the film (not as hard for a post-doc, but to be the keynote speaker as a post-doc is crazy, when there are full professors with large labs and decades of experience over you that they didn’t pick?). And, most importantly, no post-doc is that hot. Sorry, but if you’re a post-doc, you probably work ~10 hrs/day, 5-6 days a week. When are you getting jacked? Not during lab babe, sorry :( 4. Classes For most of the movie, Olive is a PhD candidate as opposed to a PhD student. This assumes her primary focus is her research and dissertation and not the Master-level classes and thesis required of early-PhD students. Yet, Olive and all of her friends are consistently seen in lectures (which also lowkey have early undergrad-level biology being explained, like the MAP-Kinase pathway). Sure, candidates can take one or two classes, but they have absolutely no reason to except pure interest, and most candidates are interested in their own research instead of learning a new subject. In fact, instead of being in class, Olive should be teaching one, which leads us to… 5. Not a TA Graduate students are typically either required or very very very much want to TA undergraduate classes, as they provide stipends that count towards your probably already-low pay as a full-time PhD. But yet again, Olive and any of her friends having to leave lab to teach is not mentioned. This wouldn’t be that big of a deal considering it would have no impact on the plot, BUT Olive is shown teaching a class for…middle schoolers? When she would have the time or requirement to do this, I don’t know. Also it was a chemistry lab, so like what? 6. Mice Olive works on blood biomarkers to detect pancreatic cancer (we’ll get to this later). As a result, she works on mice. And, in true fashion, she breaks absolutely every safety rule with mice protocols?? Most importantly, the mice are kept in the normal lab on her regular lab bench. This is, of course, not allowed. Mice terminals/rooms are required to be in separate rooms away from the traditional lab to protect the people, the mice, and the other chemicals and biologicals in the lab. Yet every time we see Olive with her mice, they’re just on the bench with other people around running other experiments. 7. PPE (Personal Protective Equipment). Gloves and a lab coat are required to be worn when touching almost anything in a lab, regardless of the lab’s safety level. Even more importantly, gloves and lab coats must be removed when leaving lab so that you don’t contaminate the outside world with anything from the lab. But dur-de-dur, none of these full-grown professors, post-docs, and PhD students follow this rule. There are full scenes where they are walking around in the hallways of the biology building with lab coats and gloves. Danger danger! 8. Working Alone It is known that Olive consistently works alone in the lab on weekends instead of going out and partying (cause she’s not like other girls etc etc.). This isn’t totally uncommon, but it is strange, and typically requires special permission from the PI since it is a safety issue to have people in the lab alone. 9. Transferring to Harvard? A large plot point throughout the movie is Olive trying to get a research position at a lab at Harvard university. This is capital-S strange. People in the movie treat this as “yay you’re getting this super cool opportunity”, which would make sense if she was a research assistant or even post-doc. But as a student, this means fully transferring programs, having to apply to Harvard, and do all that, which normally means you’re having a really negative experience in your current program and are willing to burn a bridge with your current PI over it. They do not acknowledge this. 10. Olive = Elizabeth Holmes Olive works on bio-blood markers as an early detection metric for pancreatic cancer. This is theoretically cool, but someone already did it, honey: Elizabeth Holmes. This is an actual field of study and it is valid, but I can’t help but see a blonde White woman talking about her idea to use blood to test for disease and immediately hear Elizabeth Holmes’ voice.

Title: my classes are exploding
Author: Joy X. '29
Article Content: This semester, I’m finally off the credit limit! ⁠01MIT limits the number of classes first years can take. Each full-time class is 12 units, with each unit roughly corresponding to each hour per week that you have to spend on the class, whether it is lecture, recitation, or homework. There’s nothing holding me back >:) And so this semester, I cranked the knob on the firehose ⁠02there’s a famous saying that “getting an education from MIT is like drinking from a firehose” to maximum and made the brilliantly horrible choice to register for 7 classes. They are as follows: 8.05: Quantum Mechanics II: I’m now officially a Physics major ⁠03we declared our majors at the end of first year!. I’d taken 8.04 (Quantum Mechanics I) last year, and this just seemed like the natural next step. I did have some mixed feelings about 8.04—I thought that the class was very heavy on algebra and churning numbers—but I hoped that 8.05 would give me a better understanding and appreciation. 8.033: Relativity: Another physics class; I had heard many good things about the lecturer, Scott Hughes, and they did not disappoint—he has a really engaging lecturing style and seems to care a lot about the class. In fact, our class is being recorded for MIT OpenCourseWare, so by the end of the semester, maybe the lectures will be public! 18.901: Introduction to Topology: I was actually really excited about this class. I took Algebra I and II ⁠04most people who hear this do a double take because they’re like “didn’t you take algebra i and ii in middle school??” and it’s hilarious. I’ve confused so many people with that joke. But this is the abstract algebra track, and covers things like rings, fields, linear algebra, Galois theory, etc. last year, and really enjoyed pure mathematics. I plan to declare a double major in mathematics next semester, and 18.901 is a requirement for the major. Plus, most of my previous math experience was in algebra (which I really like), and I wanted to broaden out to some analysis. 18.404: Theory of Computation: My friend took this class last year and had very high reviews of it. It looked interesting and fit in my schedule, so I added it…and to be honest, in hindsight maybe this is why my schedule exploded so much—when I was selecting classes, my philosophy was “if it fits, I’m taking it”… which looking back, was not a very good philosophy. 21G.402: German II: In high school, I really wanted to learn German. I think I just wanted to learn a language, and chose German arbitrarily because it sounded cool, I guess. I self-studied it on and off for a bit but never got too far because I was not very concentrated in my efforts. Since I had some German knowledge beforehand, I was able to skip to German II. 21G.611: Russian I: I started “learning” Russian about last year, and by “learning” I mean I had two friends who spoke Russian and I would go about asking one of them for insults in Russian to use against the other. Somehow through this I’ve gotten attached to the language, and this semester I resolved to learn more words than “дурак” ⁠05which is also the name of a popular card game in many post-Soviet countries, which is how I learned of it . 21G.086: 20th Century Ukraine and Russia: Entangled Histories and Identity Politics: All MIT students are required to take a total of 2 CI-H ⁠06Communication-Intensive Humanities subjects in their first and second years, and this is effectively our writing requirement. This was actually my second choice of CI-H—I had really wanted to take a German film class, but it had gotten unexpectedly cancelled. I had really enjoyed my history class in my senior year of high school, and was sad when we ran out of time to finish our Soviet Union unit; hence, I was excited when I saw this in the course catalogue, especially since it’s pretty relevant today. [Spoiler: I’m not in all of them anymore but somehow, for some reason, possessed by some sort of insanity, at the beginning of the semester I was fully planning to take all of them. When I met with my advisor to confirm my registration before classes started, she had (like a good advisor) expressed concern over my almost-double-the-amount-of-coursework. I therefore promised that I would drop some, but secretly I didn’t plan to. But then I did ¯\_(ツ)_/¯] This is what my schedule during the first week of classes looked like: ahhhhhh …due to some stroke of bad luck (yes yes I’m going to blame it all on luck), my classes all lined up in a row. Here’s what my first day of classes looked like: I biked ⁠07I got a bike this year! literally best investment ever; now I actually show up to lecture on time :P to Stata Center at 10:30am to get a bagged lunch before sitting in 18.901 for an hour and a half, speedwalking across campus to make it in time for 8.05, where we reviewed the material for 8.04 for one and a half hours, then scarfing down my lunch outside the lecture room (I was lucky that all the physics classes occur in the same room, 6-120, and so I had ten minutes of break where I didn’t have to relocate) before another hour and a half of lecture. Then I had a whopping thirty minutes of break! I sat in the LODGE ⁠08one of the study spaces along the Infinite Corridor, the long corridor that connects most of the buildings in MIT’s main campus and responded to some emails. I ended my academic day with an hour of Russian, where we said привет to each other for what seemed like a million times. After a total of 5.5 hours of lecture, most of them consecutively, I felt… great! I was surprised that I had held my concentration intact for such a long time, and I felt so accomplished and productive. I couldn’t wait for my problem sets to come out, so I could feel even more productive by doing them. That Sunday was a beautiful sunny day out, and I spent ten hours sitting in my room, doing my homework. Needless to say (though it was not very needless then and was quite a surprise), it was not sustainable. Although I had felt great at the start, by the end of the first full week of classes, I was getting a bad tension headache everyday from sitting in 4-4.5 hours of lecture in a row for four days in a week, then going home and spending many more hours in a row on problem sets. So I decided that if my brain was not going to overload this semester, I simply had to drop some classes. Yet even so, when I finally mustered up the strength to submit my Class Drop form, I felt some sort of separation anxiety (maybe others will call it Stockholm Syndrome). I’d psyched myself up so hard for seven classes that taking any less felt…not enough. Why did I decide to overload my schedule like this? Surely, a mix of hubris, bad foresight, and that desire to optimize everything in my life. When I was little and learning to write in Chinese, I had those workbooks of characters where you trace out characters in the book. Having been 8 or 9, at the ripe age where one learns about the Industrial Revolution in school history class, I took inspiration from the factories of the 19th century and pretended my Chinese homework was an assembly line—what happened was I wrote a row of the first strokes of some character, then went back and added the second strokes, then the third, until I had completed the page. There were some problems with this—notably, no one writes like that (imagine writing a book by writing the first letters of each word, then the second, then the third, until all your words are complete). And notably, it’s not the way you should learn to write—as a consequence, I’m still illiterate. I think the same mindset that made assembly line-ing my Chinese homework was what made me so tempted towards the Sophomore Stupid [see Anika’s blog]. I’m so tempted to treat everything in my life as something that can be optimized—like I’m a video game character and in order to win, I have to minmax my stats. When I was little, I had always measured my success comparatively—to win at life, I had to be the best in the world at something. And to be the best, I had to pour every effort in one direction. Any type of balance meant that something was wasted. I don’t mean to disparage ambition or competitiveness. I think a healthy dose of both (though at times it has not been healthy :P) has made me who I am today. But as the classic adage that I just made up goes, “Life is like riding a unicycle. To go fast, you have to not fall off.” And in order to not fall off, you need to maintain some sort of balance. ⁠09I feel like there’s also some unintended other meaning here since it’s also very hard to balance on a unicycle without going moderately fast. but ignore that :) . As it turns out, happiness is kind of important for motivation. So I ended up dropping two classes: my history class and my topology class—and poof! 12 hours of my week (and more, since problem sets also take time outside of class) were back in my possession. Here are some things I did with those extra 12 hours the next week: I watched Your Name, a movie that LSC ⁠10the Lecture Series Committee, which puts on movies on the projectors in the lecture halls every week put on. I hardly ever watch movies, but I’d heard that it was a good movie, plus my friend was running it. I had a great time! It was a really sweet movie; the art style and music was fantastic. I was sobbing at the last few scenes (I’m an easy crier—I cry at most movies that are supposed to make you cry. And sometimes at movies that are not supposed to make you cry, too ⁠11once when I was watching A Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes in the theatre I was crying of laughter so hard because one of the very emotional scenes where the main character picks up a scarf looked like he was eating a croissant ). Instead of speedrunning my bagged lunch because I had no time, now I actually had a free hour around lunchtime! I got Vietnamese Pho with a friend at Eastern Edge, a food court on the—surprise—eastern edge of campus. After a year of promising to go to Spinjam, I went to Spinjam again! Spinjam is basically firespinning, but off fire. We gather on the lawn near East Campus ⁠12a dorm at MIT , the Spinning Arts club provides lots of props and people to teach tricks on the props, and we spin things! I learned some cool tricks on the dragonstaff and tried to juggle it. Then the next week I had too many psets and skipped it again. ⁠13I promise I promiseeee I will learn to spin on fire someday After experiencing true freedom, I’ve forgotten why I wanted to take seven classes in the first place. I’ve realized that by trying to stuff my schedule with all the classes I could fit, I was missing out on so many other things. But then again, I’m always missing out on so many things—the FOMO at this school is real. Even after dropping two classes and taking “only” five classes, I’m still at a heavy courseload. It still feels like I’m rushing from assignment to assignment and from class to class. I wish I had more time to spend on my language classes—after every German class, I end up with ten or more new vocabulary words in my notebook and I keep meaning to turn them into flashcards, but it never happens. I wish I had more time to spend on my UROP ⁠14undergraduate research opportunity—I’m working on a project related to particle physics . I wish I had more time to blog. I wish I had time to juggle literally and not metaphorically. But alas, such is the curse of time that we are only allowed 24 hours in a day, 7 days in a week, and 52.1429 weeks in a year. Someday, I’ll figure out how to make a time turner, so I can go back and do everything I never had the time for.
